stories.headline: Ben Johnson and Brian Flores face off again as the Bears take on the Vikings in Week 2
stories.summary: — It's a stressful week for Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson. Same for Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores.
stories.body:
CHICAGO -- — It's a stressful week for Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson. Same for Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores.


They have that type of effect on each other.


Johnson and Flores match wits once again on Sunday when Caleb Williams and Chicago host Dallas Turner and Minnesota for their home opener. Johnson is 5-1 when calling the plays against a Flores-coached defense, averaging 27.5 points per game.


“When you go against a guy like this, you’ve got everything,” Johnson said. “So that’s where it’s a lot. For our players, they have to really dedicate themselves over the course of the week to have success on game day and fortunately I do think our guys, the way we train them is very demanding and very detailed with teams like this in mind.”


Flores, 45, is known for his array of blitzes, and he really turned up the pressure in the final part of Minnesota's 39-22 win over Green Bay in Week 1.


The Vikings trailed 22-10 in the third quarter, but they sacked Jordan Love four times in the second half. Love also lost a fumble and threw an interception in the fourth quarter. Turner was credited with a career-high seven QB hits, the most in an NFL game since Chris Jones had eight for Kansas City in Week 15 of the 2018 season.


“You’d like to think he’s put everything he could possibly do on tape until you play him next and you realize he hasn’t yet,” Johnson said. “So it’ll be something new. There always is with him and that’s what makes him such a good coordinator. It’s a great challenge. It really is.”


Johnson, 40, also presents quite the challenge for Flores and Minnesota's defense. Chicago totaled 291 yards rushing and 552 yards overall in its 59-37 victory at Carolina on Sunday. It was the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history.


“What are we getting week to week? It’s hard to know,” Flores said. “So a lot of the game is adjustments. If they do this, we want to do that. If they do that, we want to do this. And we’re going to have our own game plan to start things off. It’s the same thing on his end: What are they doing? And how are we going to counteract what they’re doing? So it’s certainly a chess match.”


Williams passed for two touchdowns and rushed for two more TDs in the first game of his second season in Johnson’s offense. The 24-year-old quarterback definitely has the Vikings' attention.


“He’s obviously capable of making highlight play after highlight play," Vikings safety Harrison Smith said. "He’s really got it all. He’s extremely talented. He’s operating that offense very well.”


Need to know
Minnesota (1-0) at Chicago (1-0).


When/where to watch: Sunday, 1 p.m. EDT, Fox.


Latest odds: Bears by 4 1/2.


Against the spread: Vikings 1-0; Bears 1-0.


Last week: Vikings beat the Packers 39-22; Bears beat the Panthers 59-37.


Last meeting: Bears beat Vikings 19-17 on Nov. 16 in Minnesota.


Series record: Vikings lead 69-59-2.


Matchup to watch
Vikings WR Justin Jefferson vs Bears CB Jaylon Johnson. Jefferson, 27, and Johnson, 27, know each other quite well. They are both 2020 draft picks who have spent their entire careers with their respective NFC North teams. Jefferson had eight catches for 92 yards and two touchdowns in Minnesota's season opener. He has 59 receptions for 790 yards and four TDs in 10 games against Chicago. Johnson is looking to bounce back from a shaky performance at Carolina. He missed both of Chicago's games against Minnesota last season. He has one interception in six games versus the Vikings.


Stats and stuff
— The Vikings have won six straight games at Soldier Field, one short of the franchise record for consecutive road wins over a division opponent. They won seven straight at Detroit from 1968-74 and seven straight on the road against Green Bay from 1971-77.


— In Week 1, the Vikings became the first team in NFL history to win by 17 or more points after trailing by 12 or more points with less than 20 minutes left in regulation, according to Stats Perform.


— Bears running back D’Andre Swift is 101 yards shy of 5,000 yards rushing for his career. The 27-year-old Swift rushed for 124 yards and three touchdowns in Week 1.


— Bears tight end Cole Kmet needs four receptions to pass Allen Robinson (293) for ninth on the franchise's career list. Kmet had two catches for 35 yards and a TD against the Panthers.


------


AP Pro Football Writer Dave Campbell contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Alex Ovechkin says he supports Russia but is 'not pro-war'
stories.summary: Alex Ovechkin is drawing criticism after appearing in a TV ad for Vladimir Putin's political party, but the NHL's career goal-scoring leader said he only "supports what's happening in Russia" and hopes the war with Ukraine will end soon.
stories.body:
NHL career goal-scoring leader Alex Ovechkin on Thursday addressed his appearance in a video for Russian President Vladimir Putin's political party, saying he accepted the government's request without hesitation, was surprised by the backlash and supports his native country while reiterating previous comments that he "is for peace and love."

"I want the peace and love for everybody," Ovechkin told ESPN. "It doesn't matter who you are, American, Russian or Ukrainian. I hope everything's gonna be good and everything's gonna be done soon."

Asked how he would explain his decision to participate in the advertisement, in which Russia's foreign minister delivered a message closely aligned with propaganda blaming Ukrainians for the invasion of their country, Ovechkin replied that he was "not pro-war." He only supports "what's happening in Russia" and hopes the war will "be done soon," he said.

Of Putin's invasion of Ukraine, Ovechkin said: "I'm not in politics. I can't say who's right and who's wrong." He added that he would support his country no matter what.

Ovechkin, 41, told ESPN that he filmed the ad three weeks ago and did not tell the Washington Capitals that he planned to participate in the campaign video before signing a one-year extension in July.

Before speaking with ESPN, Ovechkin answered questions from reporters about the video in a quiet, subdued voice before declaring, "OK, let's do hockey questions."

In the campaign video that aired in Russia earlier this month, Ovechkin stands with supporters of Putin's United Russia political party as Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov delivers a monologue warning anyone who comes at Russia "with a sword" to "expect no mercy: we will rise together, as we do today." Ovechkin, wearing a black polo shirt, stands stoically behind Lavrov.

Ovechkin's appearance earned international condemnation from critics of the regime, which has mounted an offensive against Ukraine that began in 2014 and expanded to a full-scale invasion in 2022 that has resulted in more than 1 million military and civilian casualties. In a letter to the NHL this week, Rep. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., called on the league to consider banning Ovechkin over his participation in the ad.

"While Mr. Ovechkin has every right to hold personal political views, actively participating in campaign material for Putin's oppressive party while serving as the captain of an NHL franchise in our nation's capital raises serious questions about the standards expected of players who represent the League and their communities," Wilson wrote.

The NHL did not respond to multiple requests from ESPN for comment. Likewise, the Capitals declined to answer questions concerning the video and declined to make team owner Ted Leonsis available for comment.

Earlier this week, the Capitals issued a statement noting that "Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will live there following his retirement" and that he and the team are "focused on the season ahead and the continued impact he makes on the ice and in our city."

The series of TV advertisements features more than 30 Putin supporters. One of them is Maria Lvova-Belova, a Russian official who has been involved in the kidnapping and "re-education" of Ukrainian children. Lvova-Belova, in a televised meeting with Putin, said she had personally taken a Ukrainian boy from war-ravaged Mariupol. The International Criminal Court issued a warrant for her arrest in 2023. Ovechkin stands alongside her and others in a large group shot featured in the ads.

Academic experts in Russian propaganda said Ovechkin's appearance signifies a critical victory for Putin in his bid to justify the country's costly military campaign in Ukraine. Ukrainian authorities have accused the Russian military of murdering more than 17,000 Ukrainian civilians, including more than 700 children.

"You can't look away from the fact that Russia is perpetuating a genocide on Ukrainian people," said Sarah Oates, a senior scholar in the field of political communication and democratization at the University of Maryland. "Putin has said Ukraine and Ukrainians have no right to exist. And this is a key reason for the invasion. Ovechkin supports Putin, he supports the Russian regime, and that means he supports genocide."

Asked about assertions that Russia is responsible for a genocide, Ovechkin told ESPN, "I hope it's not gonna, it's not gonna be like that," before he and a team media relations representative ended the interview.

Vitaly Kazakov, a postdoctoral researcher in media and journalism studies at Aarhus University in Denmark whose research focuses on the intersection of Russian politics and sports, said the ads amplify state messaging that absolves the Kremlin of moral responsibility in Ukraine.

"This is part of an effort to put the blame not on the Russian state, but onto external forces," he said.

In 2022, while the international sports community enacted bans on Russian athletes, the NHL supported the players, pointing to the "extremely difficult position" they had been placed in. The league said then that Russian players compete "on behalf of their NHL Clubs, and not on behalf of Russia."

Ovechkin has not appeared in United Russia campaign marketing in the past, Kazakov said.

At Thursday's Capitals media day event, coach Spencer Carbery said he didn't expect the criticism of Ovechkin to affect his place with the team.

"I know him as good as anybody inside this organization, and I know what he's all about," Carbery said. "I haven't seen the video or whatever, but I know this: He's done an amazing job in my time here. I love him, I love his family, and he's a big part of our team. Him being our captain, the relationship I have with him as a coach here, it doesn't affect that."

Ovechkin signed what is expected to be his final contract with the team -- a one-year, $4.25 million deal -- on July 2, more than two months before the ad appeared on Russian television.

The Moscow-born forward, who in April 2025 eclipsed Wayne Gretzky's all-time goals record, has been a consistent if not outspoken supporter of the Russian president throughout his career. His Instagram profile picture features himself and Putin, and he has participated in two notable social media campaigns supporting Putin's agenda. "Putin Team," in 2017, attempted to invigorate the president's approval among the country's youth. And in 2014, during Russia's initial invasion of eastern Ukraine, Ovechkin posted an Instagram photo of himself holding a sign reading "#SAVE CHILDREN FROM FASCISM." The slogan echoed Kremlin messaging that the invasion was a means of protecting Ukrainian civilians. Ovechkin later said he was not trying to make a political statement.

Throughout Ovechkin's career, Capitals officials and people close to Ovechkin have suggested in media interviews that he was under pressure from the Kremlin to support the president and could not safely criticize Putin with his family living in Russia.

In 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the then-Capitals general manager Brian MacLellan said Russian players were trying to navigate "what they can say, what they can't say," and "the repercussions that could happen back home." Of Ovechkin, he said: "He gets pressure from all sides -- from North America, from Russia, from family."

"It's a cop-out," said Slava Malamud, a Russian-born former Sport-Express hockey reporter who said the Capitals revoked his press credential in 2014 after he criticized Ovechkin's "Save Children from Fascism" post.

"All of these excuses presuppose the existence of an alternative Ovechkin no one has ever seen, one who is meekly doing what a brutal dictator tells him to do," Malamud told ESPN. "That is not an Ovechkin we have ever seen. We see a man who is proud of his president, who is standing next to war criminals.

"I don't think it's a coincidence after signing his last contract that he comes out with his unambiguous support for the war."

Pressed to comment on the invasion in 2022, Ovechkin expressed hope for peace but stopped short of condemning the decision to invade a peaceful neighbor.

"Please, no more war," Ovechkin said in 2022. "It doesn't matter who is in the war -- Russia, Ukraine, different countries. ... We have to live in peace."

Few Russian athletes, including dozens who play in the NHL, have publicly criticized the regime. Then-New York Rangers winger Artemi Panarin, born in Korkino, Russia, took the strongest anti-Putin stance among Russian NHL players in 2022, condemning political corruption in the country. Putin, he said, no longer knew the difference between right and wrong.

Getting Ovechkin's implied support, standing behind Lavrov, allows the Kremlin to downplay its banishment from the world cultural stage, Kazakov said.

"Ovechkin's persona and his achievements have been particularly important for the Kremlin in this Ukraine war period," Kazakov said. "There's this idea to make an appeal for Russia's soft power, going back to the feeling of a previous era when they hosted the Olympics and the World Cup, when their cultural figures have been prominent and beloved by people from around the world."

stories.headline: The next Shohei Ohtani? Why we haven't seen more two-way stars
stories.summary: Ohtani was supposed to be a trailblazer. Instead, his unprecedented success has reinforced just how difficult what he's doing really is.
stories.body:
SHOHEI OHTANI WASN'T supposed to remain an exception.

At one point, he was expected to be a trailblazer.

When Ohtani arrived in the major leagues as a two-way player in 2018, he was thought to be carving a path for others to follow. He wasn't just unique; he was stretching the bounds of what was possible in a sport long defined by convention. His success was potentially groundbreaking. And yet, it has occurred in a vacuum.

No other two-way players exist in the major leagues, and very few of them are being developed in the minors. Over these past eight years, while consistently performing as one of the game's best hitters and frequently taking the mound as one of its best pitchers, Ohtani has stood alone. In that time, pitching has become even more advanced, a universal designated hitter has been implemented, and breaking through as a two-way player has only grown more difficult. As it was before Ohtani, countless players who starred as hitters and pitchers at the amateur levels continue to specialize as they navigate the professional ranks.

Such as Michael Harris II, Carson Benge and Jo Adell, who were heavily scouted as pitchers but migrated to the outfield. Or Jac Caglianone and Bryce Eldridge, who were told in predraft meetings they'd have the opportunity to do both but never did. Or Jake Cronenworth and Nolan McLean, who pitched and hit in the minor leagues and left it there. Or Michael Lorenzen, who came as close as anyone but hasn't taken a major league at-bat in five years.

They've been left with wonder, but also, in some ways, relief.

"I kind of wish I would've done both," Harris, the Atlanta Braves' fifth-year center fielder, said. "At the same time, my arm doesn't hurt right now, so I'm happy with where I'm at."

Ohtani's road to being the first two-way player since Babe Ruth -- who juggled both roles when the sport was nowhere near as refined, and basically stopped pitching by the age of 25 -- has been littered with ailments, including Tommy John surgery in 2018, knee surgery in 2019, a second repair of his ulnar collateral ligament in 2023, shoulder surgery in 2024, and now, continual knee discomfort every time he toes the rubber.

Ohtani has not pitched in a game since July 3, and there's no telling when, if ever, he will again. Amid that, his offense fell off, prompting a stint on the injured list to address other ailments, most notably pain in his right arm. If Ohtani's four MVPs are a testament to what's possible when boundaries are pushed, his 2026 season is indicative of why nobody else is doing it.

Los Angeles Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes called the chances of another two-way player someday following Ohtani "close to zero."

The bar just to be a designated hitter in the major leagues is exceedingly high, Gomes noted. Meeting that threshold while juggling all the work required of starting pitchers is immensely difficult. Performing both at high enough levels to fend off the public pressure to give one of them up, as Ohtani often does, feels impossible.

"I just don't know who can do that," said Gomes, who pitched in the big leagues for five years and previously ran the Dodgers' player development department. "You have to be so highly skilled, a freak of nature physically and also mentally confident enough to be like, 'I can throw a 12-pitch bullpen at 60% to conserve my energy, and I'm more than prepared to go pitch in a game.'"

Adell played alongside Ohtani with the Los Angeles Angels for four years and often marveled at how meticulous he was with his work. Ohtani could hit balls farther and throw them harder than just about anybody, but he was also uniquely in tune with how his body was working and what it needed on a given day. The Dodgers give Ohtani more leeway than any other player because of that.

The next two-way player would need to have transcendent talent, but also, in Adell's mind, a level of precision and focus that only Ohtani seems to possess.

"I think there's going to be probably a few more to maybe attempt to do what he's done, but it's very difficult," said Adell, now with the Cleveland Guardians. "It's really the workload management part of it. Because you get halfway through the year, and you're trying to get your bullpens in, you have arm fatigue, your swing's not feeling good, but you got to do both. It's a tough task."

LORENZEN STILL THINKS about one game from seven years ago.

The Cincinnati Reds were in Pittsburgh on Sept. 27, 2019, and Lorenzen started in center field. By the seventh inning, the score was tied and Lorenzen was summoned to pitch. He held the Pirates scoreless, came to bat in the top of the eighth, drove in the go-ahead run, threw another scoreless inning in the bottom half, then went back out to center field for the ninth.

"It was college again," Lorenzen said. "It was incredible. I wish I could still do that."

Since Ohtani debuted, no major leaguer has gotten closer to replicating him than Lorenzen. With the Reds in 2019, Lorenzen compiled 83⅓ innings as a reliever and 89 innings as an outfielder. Since then, though, he has been exclusively a pitcher. He laments not getting "a long enough leash" and believes the universal DH, permanently implemented in 2022, "really screwed me." The expanded rosters instituted during the COVID-19-shortened 2020 season, which lessened the need for versatility, also didn't help.

When the Colorado Rockies signed Lorenzen to an $8 million contract this past offseason, they thought about gaining the extra roster flexibility by occasionally having him hit. But they never went through with it. Lorenzen, now a member of the Toronto Blue Jays, still hits off a pitching machine to keep his eyes acclimated to high velocity, just in case. He admits that it takes "a special mind" to be a two-way player in the major leagues, but he believes the lack of another is largely the product of a rule.

In an effort to lessen the prevalence of position players pitching, Major League Baseball began to categorize position players and pitchers in 2020 and stated that, with few exceptions, only pitchers can pitch. The rule also carved out a path for two-way status, a designation that essentially grants teams an extra pitcher. To qualify, for that season and the one after, a player needs to compile at least 20 innings as a pitcher and play at least 20 games as a position player, with at least three plate appearances in each of those games.

That last part, some players believe, is too onerous. So onerous, in fact, that it disincentivized two-way players at a time when guys such as Lorenzen, Jake Cronenworth, Jared Walsh and Matt Davidson were all aspiring to become one.

"It's unfortunate that that was the case because I think we would see a lot more guys if not for that," Cronenworth said. "It's just so hard to do it now."

An MLB official said the threshold was put in place to reward legitimate two-way players and prevent teams from leveraging the qualifications to gain two-way status by, for example, finding at-bats for pitchers in lopsided games throughout a season. The official added that the league has not heard any complaints from teams or players and is therefore not considering an adjustment to the rule.

With the Tampa Bay Rays' Triple-A affiliate in 2019, Cronenworth compiled 406 plate appearances but only made seven appearances on the mound, though he put up a 2.45 ERA. He was in the same organization that drafted Brendan McKay and Tanner Dodson as two-way players and saw it as a realistic part of his future.

Cronenworth joined the San Diego Padres in an offseason trade but was still throwing bullpens at their facility in the early part of spring training in 2020. Then the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the sport. When baseball returned, Cronenworth was strictly a position player. He hasn't pitched since.

He still thinks about what could have been.

"I know it would've been fun, that's for sure," said Cronenworth, now in his seventh season in the big leagues. "What would it have looked like? I have no idea. I was having fun and it was cool, and it was a lot."

BEFORE THE San Francisco Giants drafted Eldridge 16th out of high school in 2023, they showed him a 3D overlay of his swing and Ohtani's to show him how similar they were.

Like Ohtani, Eldridge could also pitch. As a senior at James Madison High School in Vienna, Virginia, he put up a 1.06 ERA with 66 strikeouts in 39⅔ innings on the mound and hit .422 with eight home runs and a 1.716 OPS in the batter's box.

But when he joined the Giants' minor league system, there was no pitching plan for him. He saw the writing on the wall then. A bum shoulder that materialized right around that time didn't help, either. Eldridge would occasionally remind coaches and team officials that he could pitch, but he never threw off a mound. Instead, he shot up to the big leagues as a 20-year-old first baseman last September.

"I would've loved that opportunity," Eldridge said. "I think I could've been good at it. But I'm happy where I'm at. I don't think I would be here at the age that I am if I were doing both."

Eldridge's case is the norm. As baseball becomes more difficult, its players specialize at earlier ages than ever. Even now, with teams seeing what's possible with Ohtani, the time, patience and money required to make a two-way player work in the professional ranks "would necessitate an extreme talent justification," a front office executive said.

"It's hard enough to develop starting pitching right now, much less develop a starting pitcher who also happens to be capable of hitting in a major league lineup," he added. "The talent simply doesn't exist, and even the ones that flash that type of potential get pushed to one path once they start to struggle. Ohtani isn't the guy with the torch, leading the way for others. He's the only guy. Nobody is following him."

When McKay was drafted fourth in 2017, he was considered the best two-way player to come out of college since Dave Winfield 44 years earlier. But injuries decimated his career. In the years since, only six players have been selected with a two-way designation, according to MLB's draft tracker. That number is incomplete but not by much.

There are only a handful of two-way players in the minor leagues, most of them in the lower levels. The most notable are probably Seong-Jun Kim and Josh Owens with the Texas Rangers, both of whom are in Single-A. The Athletics have one in Shotaro Morii, who also plays the infield; the Boston Red Sox have one in Conrad Cason; and the Cincinnati Reds just drafted one in Kenny Ishikawa. They're all at least three levels away from the major leagues. The chances of any of them maintaining both skill sets for very long is miniscule.

"I think people will," Benge said when asked if someone will follow Ohtani eventually. "But you also got to be the best in the world at both, so it's a pretty tough thing to do."

You also need leverage. Ohtani remained in Japan coming out of high school in 2012 because the Nippon-Ham Fighters lured him with a plan to develop him as both a pitcher and a hitter. When he finally decided to come to the United States to play in the major leagues, he picked his team based largely on who would help him be a two-way player at the world's highest level. The same occurred when he went into the free agent market after the 2023 season.

Three years later, his two-way status seems as fragile as ever.

Ohtani, who turned 32 in July, pitched like a potential Cy Young Award winner in the first half of this season, posting a 1.79 ERA in 14 starts. His production offensively continues to rank among the best in the sport, as evidenced by his 142 weighted runs created plus. But Ohtani's body has betrayed him for the better of these past three months.

Ohtani admitted last week he is "most likely" not going to pitch again this season, adding that he is "focusing on hitting moving forward." Given his age, the labor uncertainty that clouds over the sport and the overall fragility of juggling two roles simultaneously, it's probably fair to wonder if we'll ever see him pitch and hit simultaneously again. The Dodgers will basically let him try for as long as he feels capable, but nobody -- not even Ohtani himself -- knows how long that will last.

As for whether anyone will follow? That, too, is an open question.

"I think it's not the last time we see it," Eldridge said. "It's just -- I mean, that guy was built in a lab. I'm not quite sure where he came from. He's a stud. I think we'll see it in the future, especially as technology continues to get better and people have a better look at it, see how he went about his business and his routine. Maybe the coaches in Japan who helped him do that will write some sort of book or something."

ESPN's Jorge Castillo and Bradford Doolittle contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Knicks pause ticket sales after error leads to higher prices
stories.summary: The Knicks said they are pausing ticket sales after an error caused them to be listed for amounts that were too high.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- The New York Knicks said Thursday they are pausing ticket sales after an error caused them to be listed for amounts that were too high.

The NBA champions put individual game tickets for the 2026-27 season on sale this week. The get-in price for the Oct. 20 season opener against Philadelphia was more than $1,000.

"We are pausing Knicks individual ticket sales due to a mistake in our pricing. We are rolling back to last year's prices plus an average increase of 12%. We will restart sales with new prices shortly, and anyone who already purchased individual tickets will be refunded the difference," Madison Square Garden Sports said in a statement.

There is generally a ticket increase after seasons when the Knicks made the playoffs. Owner James Dolan has not raised them when the team does not.

"Our intention was never to overcharge our loyal fans, and we thank everyone for their support of the Knicks and their patience as we get this right," MSG said.

stories.headline: UFC 331 preview and picks: Pantoja sees opportunity in disaster
stories.summary: Top storylines and coaches' analysis for UFC 331 in Los Angeles.
stories.body:
For two and a half years, Alexandre Pantoja ruled the UFC's flyweight division at a level unseen since the historic era of Demetrious Johnson nearly 10 years ago. And yet, the past nine months since his last fight could prove to be the most compelling of Pantoja's career.
The 36-year-old Pantoja (30-6) will challenge Joshua Van (17-2) for the 125-pound championship at UFC 331 inside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Saturday. It will be his first appearance since UFC 323 in December, when he lost the belt to Van via TKO after Pantoja suffered a dislocated elbow 26 seconds into the fight. The nature of the loss has led to a feeling of unfinished business between the two fighters going into Saturday's main event.

"As an athlete, yes, I have a TKO loss on my record," Pantoja told ESPN. "I've never lost by TKO or submission before. Nobody had ever finished me. Now, I have that. But personally, as a man? No. I don't believe I have a loss to him."

Pantoja won the title against Brandon Moreno in 2023 and defended the belt four times before meeting Van. He was among the best pound-for-pound fighters in the world at the time. But with a comeback narrative attached to him for this fight, he said there is an added level of excitement.

"For sure, this is an opportunity," Pantoja said. "In my soul, that's the opportunity. Now, I get to fight the champion. He's the champion of the world and I love that. It makes the fight more spicy for me."

Van, 24, has embraced the narrative -- even while cementing himself as the undisputed champion. There are those who say Van needs to defeat Pantoja again to legitimize his championship, but Van's first title defense against Tatsuro Taira in May made discrediting him harder. Taira's ground game posed a real threat to Van, but he ultimately knocked out the Japanese challenger in the fifth round of a matchup that earned fight of the night honors at UFC 328.

The unfinished business, Pantoja's return and Van's undeniable star power mean Saturday's flyweight title fight is shaping up to be the most anticipated 125-pound title fight since Henry Cejudo ended Johnson's nearly five-year title reign in 2018 then defended the flyweight belt against then-bantamweight champion TJ Dillashaw in 2019.

For Pantoja specifically, his worst stroke of bad luck could turn into the greatest night of his career.

"Saturday night is going to be my best night, man," Pantoja said. "I haven't been to work in 10 months. That's why all of these fights, and this one especially, is worth so much. We work for months to just get one night of work. I've recovered my arm. Now I have an opportunity to show everyone what I did in the last 10 months."

More storylines to watch
History isn't in Pantoja's favor
If Alexandre Pantoja is searching for role models to inspire this weekend's quest to reclaim the championship he lost suddenly and painfully last December, he would be wise to look beyond recent history.

Within the past two weeks, two of the UFC's 11 champs -- women's flyweight Valentina Shevchenko and heavyweight Tom Aspinall -- vacated their titles because of health issues. Their paths back to the top of the mountain are as yet uncharted.

Before them, the most recent champions to lose their titles to injuries did not fare well upon their returns. In November 2022, Jiří Procházka vacated the UFC light heavyweight title after hurting his shoulder in training. His successor was Jamahal Hill, who just months after winning the vacant title had to vacate it himself after rupturing an Achilles. As soon as he was healed, Hill was granted an opportunity to reclaim his title and lost. Procházka was given three shots at the 205-pound belt and fell short in all of them.

For a success story, Pantoja must look deeper into UFC championship history to the brutal health issues overcome by Dominick Cruz. While preparing for a bantamweight title defense in May 2012, Cruz tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee. He underwent surgery, then had a setback requiring a second ACL surgery six months later. He was scheduled to return in February 2014 but suffered a groin tear in training. Facing another extended recovery, he vacated his title.

Cruz returned that September and won a fight that put him in position for a shot at his old belt. Three months later, he tore his other ACL.

Finally, in February 2016 -- more than four years after his last title fight -- Cruz challenged TJ Dillashaw for the belt and won a split decision. "I had to show something to myself," Cruz said afterward. "That's what this was."

Tsarukyan's chance to set things right again
Arman Tsarukyan was labeled a snubbed man after it was announced that Justin Gaethje and Paddy Pimblett would headline the first UFC card of 2026 with the No. 1 lightweight contender status at stake. It's hard to remember that sentiment now, considering the year Tsarukyan has had.

In the absence of an obvious UFC fight to take, Tsarukyan has wrestled competitively -- mostly in RAF -- 10 times in 2026. He raised his social media presence exponentially behind videos of lavish cars, extraordinary meals and collaborations with content creator Nina Drama. This is the longest layoff of his UFC career, but his brand has grown more during that time off than from any single fight.

He appears in a good position to get back to work and finally earn the title shot many have said he should have already had. But it won't be an easy fight. Tsarukyan's opponent, Mauricio Ruffy, is a dangerous underdog (+270, according to DraftKings). This fight will restore the order the top of the 155-pound division has lacked in Tsarukyan's absence, regardless of who wins.

Another step for Steveson?

Any MMA prospect would almost certainly switch places with 26-year-old UFC newcomer Gable Steveson. When you're an Olympic gold medal wrestler, and one of the most touted heavyweight prospects in MMA history, certain opportunities are going to come to you that others aren't afforded. It also means Steveson's window for error is small, as he's asked to learn and develop under the sport's brightest lights.

The UFC is managing his opposition. For his second UFC appearance (and fifth pro fight overall), he'll take on Sean Sharaf, a 33-year-old with two knockout losses in his first two UFC fights. Steveson will once again be a heavy, heavy favorite (-2100 by DraftKings), as he was for his promotional debut in July. The heavyweight division is wide open now that Tom Aspinall has vacated his title and the list of top contenders is thin, so Steveson's performance probably means more than the result. If he continues to look the part, his career trajectory could be accelerated at a rate few see.

Coaches' questions and predictions
"Can Pantoja bank enough rounds on the ground, while staying responsible on the feet?"

What a fight this will be. Van shows up in big moments; he's just a proven gamer. If Pantoja stands with Van, he's going to get hurt. Pantoja is good at applying pressure and landing the 1-2 punch (lead left jab, right cross), but he cannot play that game with Van, because of Van's counterboxing. Van's hands are too fast. Van can land four-to-six shots at a time in close distance, and that's something Pantoja really has to watch for. Van is going to have confidence in his ability to get off the ground from his last fight against Taira. I'm going to stay on the fence and say it's a pick 'em. After watching Van's fight with Taira, though, knowing how good Taira is on the ground, it's a little unfair to say Van can't weather the storm on the ground with Pantoja. -- Sayif Saud, Fortis MMA

Prediction: Too close to call

"How big of a setback is Pantoja's injury at age 36?"
Van is young, fired up and he's got bricks in his hands. We've seen some small weaknesses in his game, which are obviously due to lack of experience. He's getting better all the time. If Pantoja comes back and is anywhere close to where he was when he was holding the belt, I think he gets it back. There are just too many variables on the ground. We saw Van get mounted by Taira. Van is going to go to work on fixing that hole in his game, but Pantoja is so good. The biggest question is how bad of a setback is Pantoja's injury, at this stage of his career? He's not a spring chicken. But if he's the same Pantoja, he gets the win, potentially by submission. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Prediction: Pantoja by decision or submission

"Can Ruffy stop takedowns and keep space?"

Arman has been on such a tear with the wrestling in RAF, showing his ability to wrestle bigger guys and show his power and skill in grappling. When it comes to that, he is very dangerous. Ruffy is finding his groove, and he's very sharp on the feet, but former opponents King Green and Michael Chandler don't pose the same grappling threat that Arman poses. I think Benoît Saint Denis kind of exposed that hole in Ruffy's game. It's not to say Ruffy doesn't have a chance. In space, he is a problem. He can absolutely starch Arman in space. But how does he keep a powerhouse like Arman at distance? -- Saud

Prediction: Tsarukyan by decision

"Has Ruffy improved his ground defense enough?"
This is a really interesting fight. Arman is going to want to grind out Ruffy. Arman is easily a top-five wrestler/grappler in the UFC. The one thing about Arman -- even though he's stayed busy with the wrestling appearances, he's been out of the UFC for a while, so it'll be interesting to see how he looks. But unless Ruffy catches him and knocks him out, Arman is a good striker, too. Arman can go the distance in a hard fight. My gut leans to Arman. I'm a big fan of Ruffy, but it's just that grappling prowess of Arman. -- Wood

Prediction: Tsarukyan by decision

ESPN's Jeff Wagenheim contributed to this story.

stories.headline: Michail Antonio found guilty of failing to identify driver of his Lamborgini to police
stories.summary: Michail Antonio has been found guilty of failing to identify the driver of his Lamborghini supercar when it was suspected of involvement in a motoring offence in central London.
stories.body:
Michail Antonio has been found guilty of failing to identify the driver of his Lamborghini supercar when it was suspected of involvement in a motoring offence in central London.

The former West Ham striker, 36, was charged by the Metropolitan Police with failing to assist an investigation when his car had been spotted being driven without due care and attention late at night in Pall Mall last November.

Antonio told Uxbridge Magistrates' Court he was not the driver that night, having allowed his Lamborghini to be loaned out by his cousin while he was away in Manchester.

He claimed he had not received the initial police letter, asking for the driver's identity, suggesting it was lost in the post.

And he gave evidence that he was "shocked" to discover, in February, that he had been charged with a failure to identify the driver.

Antonio told the court he left his cousin to reply to the charge, and believes he then provided details of the guilty driver.

But after a short trial, Antonio was found guilty by magistrates of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of a vehicle when required.

Magistrate Ian Comfort said the panel was sure the police letter had arrived, and found that Antonio had failed to respond according to the legal requirements.

Antonio already has six penalty points on his licence, after being convicted of driving without insurance in July 2025. He now faces the prospect of an automatic driving ban.

Antonio was the registered keeper of the Lamborghini Urus when it was involved in an incident on Pall Mall at 12.38 a.m. on Nov. 5 last year.

The Met wrote to him on Nov. 12 last year to seek the identity of the driver, and commenced a criminal prosecution when it did not receive a response.

Giving evidence, Antonio said he was visiting his children in Manchester from Nov. 3 to 6 last year, and said he had handed over the keys to the Lamborghini to Tarique Josephs who runs a company loaning out cars.

He said he called Josephs in February after receiving a notice of the criminal charge.

"I was in shock", Antonio said, of his reaction to finding out he was being prosecuted. "How can I be charged with something I haven't done?

"This is the first time I was aware of that."

He gave evidence that Josephs "rents my car every now and then", telling the court: "When someone calls up for a Lamborghini, he will call me and say can I use your Lamborghini.

"I worked out he had the car at the time, he has come across to me to collect the forms, and said he would send the details."

Josephs told the court he filled out the response to the prosecution, entering a not guilty plea and giving a brief explanation that the car had been on loan.

When questioned why he had not mentioned the other driver's details on the form, he claimed to have included a copy of the loan agreement in the same envelope when posting it back.

Antonio's girlfriend, Sunita Bains, gave evidence that she handles the mail to their £2.2 million Buckinghamshire mansion, and said she does not believe the initial police letter ever arrived.

The striker is also accused of failing to respond to West Midlands police over a speeding offence in the Lamborghini. He is set to stand trial on that charge next March.

Antonio's footballing career was derailed in December 2024 when he crashed a Ferrari in Epping Forest in Essex, suffering a badly broken leg.

The Jamaica international spent three weeks in hospital and was out of the game recovering from his injuries for more than half a year.

Antonio, who has played for Reading, Sheffield Wednesday and Nottingham Forest, became West Ham's top scorer in the Premier League during his 10 years at the club.

He left in summer 2025, joining Al Sailiya in Qatar where he made four appearances before signing for Watford on a free transfer earlier this month.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton shuts down asking Ferrari to make changes: 'Never asked for anyone to be replaced'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton denied he has called for replacements at Ferrari after he admitted his bid for a record eight world championship is over.
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton denied he has called for replacements at Ferrari after he admitted his bid for a record eighth world championship is over.

Hamilton threw in the title towel at last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix after he retired from the race in Madrid with a brake problem.

His failure to finish leaves him 101 points behind Kimi Antonelli in the championship standings -- the equivalent of more than four victories -- with just nine scheduled rounds left.

A report in Italy claimed Hamilton has challenged Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur to make changes to the team's trackside staff.

But in a story posted to his Instagram account on Thursday, the 41-year-old wrote: "I've seen some of the stories that have gone out and I want to clear it up on here.

"I've never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced. Everyone I work with works hard every day, and their dedication is what moves us forward.

"I always try to empower and lift people to be the best versions of themselves or at least see the best in themselves.

"I may not always achieve that but it's my intention and what I'm here to do. We all work together and that will continue."

- Lando Norris backs 'exciting' 2027 Monaco GP sprint weekend but 'tougher for us drivers'

- Max vs 100: Verstappen jokes taking on '200' drivers next time after winning crazy challenge

- F1 2027 calendar: Monaco GP gets sprint race, Türkiye and Portugal return to schedule

Hamilton sparked hope of challenging Antonelli -- the driver who replaced him at Mercedes -- when he won in Barcelona in June.

However, the British driver has not finished on the podium at the past five rounds and has been openly critical of his team's race tactics.

He also took aim at teammate Charles Leclerc's driving after an opening-lap clash in Monza earlier this month. Hamilton said he led face-to-face talks with the Monegasque to clear the air.

His retirement in Madrid marked his first of the campaign, and when asked to assess his title chances, Hamilton replied: "There's no stopping him [Antonelli] and Mercedes this year. They've done a phenomenal job, and they deserve it [the championship]."

stories.headline: Borussia Dortmund teenager Konstantinos Karetsas returns to training after Champions League health scare
stories.summary: Borussia Dortmund says 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.
stories.body:
Borussia Dortmund have said 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.

Karetsas passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass during Dortmund's 3-2 win over Villarreal on Sept. 8.

He was in tears as he was stretchered off with suspected circulatory problems and was then taken to a hospital, where he stayed for much of last week.

"Konstantinos Karetsas is back in team training as of Wednesday after doing individual sessions at the start of the week," Dortmund said. "It was his first joint session with his teammates after he was taken off with circulatory problems in the game against Villarreal."

Dortmund hasn't specified the nature of any diagnosis for Karetsas, who was signed from Genk for a reported fee of $34.6 million last month, and didn't indicate whether he would be able to play Saturday against Stuttgart in the Bundesliga.

Karetsas plays internationally for Greece but was born in Belgium, where local media have reported that dehydration was suspected as a factor.

"I'm doing really well," he said in a video recorded during a visit to his old club Genk and published Monday on X. "We tested everything and everything is fine. I just need to adjust a bit to the intensity but that will come with time."

"I went out with him but in that moment, he wasn't able to speak," Book said.

Karetsas was able to cheer on his teammates from the stands in Saturday's 3-0 win over Paderborn.

Managing director Lars Ricken said there had been "no warning signs" of any circulatory problems prior to the incident.

stories.headline: NRL Midweek Mail semifinals: Bulldogs move to lock away rising rookie
stories.summary: Ronaldo Mulitalo is determined to honour his departing Sharks teammates, Sione Katoa has opened up about his future at the Cowboys and his finals days at the Sharks, while Nathan Cleary is fighting the clock to be fit for Penrith's prelim.
stories.body:
The NRL rarely stands still.

Between training sessions, media appearances, and behind-the-scenes conversations, new storylines often begin to emerge before the weekend arrives.

Throughout the week, ESPN will be gathering notes, insights, and updates from around the competition heading into the NRL's semifinal week.

Bulldogs move early to lock down rising forward

The Bulldogs have moved early to lock down rising forward Alekolasimi 'AJ' Jones, with the club's Rookie of the Year agreeing to a two-year contract extension.

ESPN understands Jones, who was already contracted through the 2027 season, has agreed to a new deal that will keep him at Belmore beyond his existing contract.

The move ensures Jones' future is secured before he would have been free to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 from November 1.

Kennedy backs Hynes amid criticism

Will Kennedy believes Nicho Hynes has grown from the criticism that has followed him throughout his career, praising the Sharks star ahead of their semi-final against the Roosters.

"He's learned a lot from all the criticism he gets and he's taken a step forward," Kennedy said. "For me, I just want to get around him because he's my brother and I want to play next to him."

Trindall 'really good' after shoulder scare

Will Kennedy says Braydon Trindall has pulled up well after battling through a shoulder issue in Cronulla's finals win over North Queensland.

Kennedy said Trindall had been "really dialled in on the mental side" of his game and indicated the halfback had told him he was feeling "really good" ahead of the Roosters clash.

Mulitalo relishing 'Marky Mark' rematch

Ronaldo Mulitalo is embracing another blockbuster battle with Roosters star Mark Nawaqanitawase, describing the departing winger as a "generational talent".

Mulitalo said Nawaqanitawase "brings the best out of me" and revealed their on-field rivalry is largely one-sided when it comes to the verbal exchanges.

"He's a gentleman out there... he doesn't really say anything. I think it's more myself," Mulitalo joked. "He knows I'm just going to keep talking, so he just ignores me anyway."

Mulitalo determined to honour departing Sharks

Ronaldo Mulitalo says Cronulla's finals run carries added significance with several longtime teammates set to leave the club at season's end.

Mulitalo said he has played alongside some of the departing Sharks since he was 16 and wants to "honour those boys" with his performance against the Roosters.

"I don't want to let them down and disappoint them, winning the game is the most important part of the week for me."

Katoa reveals Cowboys appeal

Sione Katoa has revealed North Queensland's attacking style was a major attraction behind his move to the Cowboys in 2027.

After helping eliminate his future club from the finals, Katoa told ESPN he "loves the style of footy" they play, describing it as "free footy" and similar to Cronulla's attack.

Katoa emotional over Sharks farewell
He also admitted the reality that every game could be his last for Cronulla is beginning to sink in.

"Tonight might have been the last week, maybe the last game," he told ESPN after scoring a double against North Queensland.

"I'm very happy right now that I get another week with my brothers and play again."

Cleary racing clock for preliminary final

Nathan Cleary is in doubt for Penrith's preliminary final after scans revealed an stress-related bone issue in his foot.

The Panthers will assess and monitor their star halfback over the next fortnight, with their week off providing valuable recovery time.

Cleary has, however, been cleared of any suspension concern after receiving only a Grade 1 Dangerous Contact charge for his incident with Hugo Savala.

stories.headline: Patriots' TreVeyon Henderson says he's 'ready to go' for Week 2
stories.summary: Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson said Thursday he's "ready to go" for Sunday's game against the Steelers after missing New England's opener with an ankle injury.
stories.body:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson, who missed the season opener due to an ankle injury, is set to return for Sunday's home opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

"I'm ready to go. Thank God I'm healed up now," Henderson said Thursday. "I'm excited to be back out here with my teammates."

The speedy Henderson, who totaled nine rushing touchdowns in his 2025 rookie season, injured his right ankle in practice Aug. 24. He complements starting running back Rhamondre Stevenson, who was on the field for 60 of 71 offensive snaps in the season-opening 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks.

Henderson returned to practice this week. He was a full participant Wednesday and his ankle responded well.

"I'm thankful. It just continued to draw me closer to the Lord, and I'm thankful for the time, thankful for the growth," he said of the time on the sideline. "I wanted to be out there [last week] pretty bad, it was a good matchup, good game, I think we competed really hard."

Henderson played in all 17 regular-season games last season and totaled 180 carries for 911 yards and nine touchdowns, while adding 35 receptions for 221 yards and one receiving touchdown.

stories.headline: GM: 'Door open' for star goalie Hellebuyck to remain with Jets
stories.summary: Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff didn't rule out the possibility that goaltender Connor Hellebuyck could remain with the team after going public with a trade demand. The Jets formally suspended Hellebuyck on Wednesday for failure to report to training camp.
stories.body:
Winnipeg Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff didn't rule out the possibility that star goaltender Connor Hellebuyck could remain with the team after going public with a trade demand.

The Jets formally suspended Hellebuyck on Wednesday for failure to report to training camp. The 33-year-old goaltender requested a trade during exit interviews after last season, his 11th with the franchise. Hellebuyck won the Hart Trophy as NHL MVP in 2025 and has won the Vezina Trophy as the NHL's top goaltender three times, being a finalist for the award five times.

"No doors are closed. He's a player that's under contract for five years. But at the end of the day, that's his choice," said Cheveldayoff at the opening of training camp on Thursday.

Cheveldayoff said there's no timeline for trading his star goaltender, something the Jets have been trying to do for "a long period of time," including during last June's NHL draft. While he pushed back on a report this week that categorized the offers for Hellebuyck as "terrible," the Jets GM said, "There's been nothing that's allowed us to say, 'OK, this works for both teams.'"

Hellebuyck and his agent made their trade demand public with a statement in late August, saying "I have tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options" in trading him.

"When Connor requested being traded, we kept it quiet. That was partly on his request as well. And we tried to make that work and we've been trying to make that work ever since," Cheveldayoff said.

There's been a wave of speculation about why Hellebuyck has asked out of Winnipeg just two seasons into a seven-year contract extension that he signed in Oct. 2023.

Cheveldayoff was asked about comments Hellebuyck made about the "blowback" his wife Andrea received after the goaltender led Team USA to Olympic gold in the 2026 Winter Olympics over Team Canada. Hellebuyck attended the State of the Union Address with all but five of his teammates, where President Donald Trump announced that the goalie would be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

"What they endured, they shouldn't have had to," said Cheveldayoff of the social media abuse.

TSN reported this week that Hellebuyck will not waive his no-movement clause to join any of the six other Canadian NHL teams.

"I'm not going to get into the specific teams. My guess is to what his restrictions are in those regards. Again, the choices that he makes are the choices that he makes. I don't have an understanding as to why he made some of the choices that he made when talking about those kind of situations," Cheveldayoff said.

There's also been speculation about a "gentlemen's agreement" that might have been made between Cheveldayoff and Hellebuyck when the goalie re-signed in Winnipeg, that if he asked out during his contract, that request would be honored.

"A contract is a contract in the National Hockey League, period. There are no side agreements, there's no general agreements. The league doesn't allow for that. So I guess the fact is any notion around that would not have any merit," Cheveldayoff said.

The Jets GM was also asked if there was a "promise" made to Hellebuyck and Jets star center Mark Scheifele that the team would contend for the Stanley Cup annually when both players signed their extensions in Oct. 2023.

"Promise is an interesting word. We've been a team that's tried to be as competitive as we possibly can each and every year," he said.

But overall, the Jets GM wasn't looking to explore why Hellebuyck wanted out.

"I guess in my mind it's irrelevant. In my mind, I have to deal with the situation that's in front of me. Connor's made the choices and we'll just deal with him moving forward," he said.

The Jets GM addressed the challenge in trying to move Hellebuyck. Beyond finding a deal that helps Winnipeg stay competitive and Hellebuyck's trade protection, Cheveldayoff said it's a smaller market when trying to trade a No. 1 goalie vs. other positions.

"If you're a team that has a bona fide No. 1 goaltender and he's locked up and he's yours, you're probably not interested. And it's not disparaging Connor Hellebuyck or anything like that. It's just the goalie market in general," he said. "So the fact of the matter that a team might be on the list as an available option has a No. 1 goaltender, well, that's kind of a moot point."

Hellebuyck will begin losing salary if he's still suspended when the NHL regular season starts. His $8.5 million average annual value will not count against the Jets' salary cap.

stories.headline: Toronto Raptors offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: With Leonard and Barnes, the Raptors are hoping to bring the franchise back to title contention. Question is: Do they have enough in a stronger East to do it?
stories.body:
The Raptors' road to real Eastern Conference contention opened in earnest Monday, when Toronto and the LA Clippers finally hit send on their long-delayed trade that will send seven-time All-Star Kawhi Leonard to Toronto for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, one first-round pick swap and two second-round picks.

The trade ends a saga that enveloped both teams, as the NBA completed its nearly year-long investigation into allegations of salary cap circumvention stemming from the Clippers' dealings with Leonard over the course of his tenure in Los Angeles.

Now with Leonard in Toronto, the two-time Finals MVP will pair with rising star Scottie Barnes and second-year big Collin Murray-Boyles, hoping to replicate the success of their title run in 2019.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season, with 30 previews -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Friday. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more.

Key retentions: Jamal Shead

After waiting months to finalize their acquisition of Leonard from the Clippers because of the NBA's investigation into salary cap circumvention, the Raptors can finally look ahead to what could be their most promising season in years.

Leonard, who led Toronto to the 2019 championship, plugs in as a major positional upgrade over Ingram. The rest of the Raptors' starting lineup remains intact, and forward Collin Murray-Boyles should only improve after a standout rookie campaign.

While losing Mamukelashvili in free agency took a bite out of their bench unit, Toronto has crafted a high-energy and versatile supporting cast for Leonard and two-time All-Star Scottie Barnes.

The plucky Raptors, who won 46 games last season, have a real shot to win their first playoff series since 2020. -- Ben Golliver

Zach Kram's offseason grade: A

Toronto's only real move of consequence this summer was trading for Kawhi Leonard, who should bring major improvements over Brandon Ingram on both ends -- especially offense, where Leonard is the sort of primary option and half-court scorer whom the previous version of the Raptors lacked.

The cost in draft picks was substantially greater than the last time Toronto traded for Leonard, eight years ago, but it was a worthwhile risk for a team that now has a legitimate chance to reach the Finals if Leonard can stay healthy next season. That gamble worked out eight years ago, after all. -- Kram

What we learned this offseason
The Raptors had two good reasons to go through with the Kawhi Leonard trade.

After enjoying a 16-win jump in the standings and snapping a three-year playoff drought, the Raptors entered the summer with a bunch of big contracts on their books and limited avenues to take the next step.

The simplest path to improvement involved packaging either Immanuel Quickley or Brandon Ingram along with other players or picks for positional upgrades. Given the hearty salaries owed to Quickley and Ingram, that wasn't going to be an easy task. But the Raptors managed to construct exactly this type of trade by sending Ingram, Gradey Dick, two first-round picks, a first-round swap and two second-round picks to the LA Clippers for Kawhi Leonard.

The primary goal of the deal, of course, was to bring Leonard back to the organization he led to the 2019 title. With a two-time Finals MVP in place, Toronto could feel much more comfortable against the East's elite and start dreaming about winning its first playoff series since 2020.

The trade's other huge benefit was shedding Ingram's contract. The two-time All-Star disappeared during the 2026 playoffs, and he is owed $40 million in 2026-27 and $41.9 million in 2027-28.

While trading for Ingram in 2025 and subsequently re-signing him were both ill-advised decisions, flipping him for Leonard amounted to a brilliant use of the undo button.

The long-discussed Leonard trade was finally consummated Monday after the NBA completed its investigation into allegations of salary cap circumvention. Once the league office announced that Leonard's punishment was limited to a $700,000 fine, Toronto was able to proceed with a bold move that added talent and fixed a past mistake. -- Golliver

The big question: How high is Scottie Barnes' ceiling?
Barnes' impressive growth shouldn't get lost in all the hubbub over Leonard's arrival.

The 2021 lottery pick really came into his own during his age-24 season, improving his scoring efficiency, earning his first All-Defensive Team selection and raising his game against the Cleveland Cavaliers in the playoffs.

While the Raptors lost their first-round series in seven games, Barnes averaged 24.1 points, 6.1 rebounds, 8.6 assists, 1.1 steals and 1.7 blocks per game -- a level of all-around playoff production matched only by LeBron James, Nikola Jokic and Cade Cunningham over the past decade.

Barnes should be regarded as one of the leading Defensive Player of the Year candidates, and he just might pop up on future MVP ballots if his upward trajectory and Toronto's winning ways continue. -- Golliver

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 14
Here are the predicted net points per 100 possessions for the Raptors' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

Kawhi Leonard shot 6.8 3-pointers per game last year, a career high, at 39%, below what he shot in each of the four prior seasons. But the extra volume meant he added plus-1.9 net points per 100 possessions on 3s vs. plus-1.6 in prior years. That's not a huge bump, but it's relevant.

Also, Leonard is one of those rare players whose college 3-point percentage was really low (25%), only to shoot really well in the NBA (39%). -- Dean Oliver

Read about how net points works here.

Biggest X factor this season
PF Collin Murray-Boyles

Ever since the Raptors agreed to acquire Leonard from the Clippers, thoughts of the Leonard/Barnes/Murray-Boyles defensive trio have tantalized. That's the key group and lineup combination that could propel the Raptors to lofty heights this season.

So even though Murray-Boyles is only a second-year player who averaged 8.5 points as a rookie, he profiles as one of the biggest X factors in the league.

For the Raptors to maximize their window with Leonard, they need Murray-Boyles to take greater steps this season and prove his bona fides as a small-ball center who can replace Jakob Poeltl in clutch situations. -- Kram

stories.headline: Alexa Grasso shows off flyweight's elite status in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Former UFC champion puts elite status of women's flyweight division on display in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
It's uncommon for two fighters ranked in the pound-for-pound top 10 to meet in a bout with no championship at stake. But that was the case at Saturday's fourth annual Noche UFC, where Alexa Grasso faced Manon Fiorot.

Grasso is a former women's flyweight champion and Fiorot competed for the belt last year, so their status as MMA elites was well established before they fought. And when Grasso won by unanimous decision, she further solidified her standing in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound rankings.

The top five of the rankings remains intact, and Grasso moves up from 10th to replace Fiorot at No. 6. Fiorot slips two positions to No. 8 in a pound-for-pound hierarchy in which seven of the 10 ranked women compete at flyweight (including Zhang Weili, the former UFC strawweight champion who last fought in an unsuccessful challenge of Valentina Shevchenko in November).

With Shevchenko injured and having vacated her title, there will be much scrambling for the top spot, which will be at stake when No. 5 Natalia Silva fights unranked Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Sept. 16. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which will be up for grabs when Natalia Silva meets Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

5. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight

Record: 20-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Rose Namajunas, Jan. 24

Next: Oct. 3 vs. Wang Cong

Silva is looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Namajunas at UFC 324. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027. With an injured Valentina Shevchenko having vacated the title, Silva will fight Wang for the belt at UFC 332.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her October bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Cris Cyborg; 5. Alexa Grasso; 6. Manon Fiorot; 7. Dakota Ditcheva; 8. Natalia Silva; 9. Erin Blanchfield; 10. Tatiana Suarez.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Zhang; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Blanchfield.

Andrew Davis: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Blanchfield; 8. Ditcheva; 9. Suarez; 10. Fiorot.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Fiorot; 10. Suarez.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Suarez; 10. Ditcheva.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

5. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

6. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (37) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Alexandre Pantoja

UFC flyweight

Record: 30-6

Last: L (TKO1) vs. Joshua Van, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Sept. 19 vs. Joshua Van

Pantoja became the UFC's unquestioned flyweight king by racking up four title defenses, including two in pay-per-view main events in 2024. He built his winning streak to eight in his UFC 317 win over Kai Kara-France, whom he had already defeated before, like other challengers. But he lost his belt in a gruesome way, injuring his elbow in the opening seconds of a UFC 323 fight with Van. Pantoja gets his rematch with Van at UFC 331.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight interim champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight. Gane was heralded as the future of the generation when he broke onto the scene, but endured growing pains in losses to Ngannou and Jones. He looks formidable now, and no one will be counting him out if he faces Aspinall in a title unification bout.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight / light heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: TBA

He was on the verge of making history when the opportunity fell apart. Pereira was a UFC champion at middleweight, then light heavyweight, but his unprecedented pursuit of a belt in a third weight class did not go well for the Brazilian, who lost an interim heavyweight title fight to Gane on the White House card. At 39 years old, Pereira does not have much time left to recapture the magic.

Other fighters receiving votes: Joshua Van and Arman Tsarukyan.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Merab Dvalishvili; 4. Ilia Topuria; 5. Alexander Volkanovski; 6. Ciryl Gane; 7. Tom Aspinall; 8. Arman Tsarukyan; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Alexandre Pantoja.
