Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Pantoja; 4. Yan; 5. Gaethje; 6. Dvalishvili; 7. Topuria; 8. Gane; 9. Pereira; 10. Volkanovski.

stories.headline: Fantasy women's hoops: Finish the job and win the fantasy finals with these picks
stories.summary: The final edition of weekly picks take you from the WNBA's return to the end of the fantasy women's hoops finals.
stories.body:
The daily news and notes around the WNBA have actionable value when applied to fantasy women's basketball. From lineup changes to hot streaks to injury news, check this page regularly for updates from ESPN's fantasy analysts Eric Moody and André Snellings.

Resources: Rankings | Scoring leaders | Added/dropped | ESPN Fantasy app

Sept. 17: Four players to target in free agency

Andre Snellings: The FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup has concluded, with Team USA staging a massive comeback in the championship game to bring home the gold. The tournament caused a break in the WNBA season right in the middle of the fantasy playoffs, but the break ends on Thursday when the season resumes... with the WNBA at an interesting junction.

All eight playoffs teams are already clinched, but there is plenty of room for teams to move up and down in the standings. In addition, teams will want to enter the postseason on a high note so they will need to play themselves back into form after the layoff. In addition, many of the player contracts signed after last offseason's Collective Bargaining Agreement were for a single year, so a large chunk of the league are effectively in contract years. So, even if a player's team may be out of the playoffs hunt, they may still have quite a bit to play for going into the offseason.

As always, we help you keep your team operating at its best by pointing out some players that may be available on your free agency wire that are performing well enough to be worthy of rostering or streaming.

Sydney Taylor, G, Chicago Sky (Rostered in 34.5% of ESPN Leagues): Taylor was one of the hotter scorers in the WNBA for most of the month of July, when she averaged 19.3 PPG during a 10-game stretch from July 7 through Aug. 1 before injuries slowed her down. She returned from a five-game absence for the end of August but was playing more limited minutes. The layoff gave her time to get healthier for the end of the season which could allow her to finish on another upswing.

Awa Fam, C, Seattle Storm (46.4%): With Ezi Magbegor (knee) out for the season, Fam may be asked to take a larger role for the Storm moving forward. The 20-year-old rookie has had some strong performances in her rookie season and has nightly double-double potential when getting near-starter minutes.

Awak Kuier, C, Dallas Wings (35.4%): Kuier has started six of the last seven games for the Wings with an expanded role since Azzi Fudd went down for the season. Kuier is one of the best shot-blockers and defenders in the league, averaging 3.3 BPG and 1.0 SPG along with a near double-double of 8.7 PPG and 7.4 RPG during that seven game stretch.

Lexi Held, G, Phoenix Mercury (1.4%): Held got a spot start in place of Kahleah Copper in the game before the break and turned in 11 points with three steals and three 3-pointers in 21 minutes. With both Kelsey Plum (leg) and Jovana Nogic (overseas commitment) out for the season, Held is likely to remain a starter for the remainder of the campaign and continue to be a solid source of scoring and 3-point shooting.

2026 fantasy women's basketball awards

Eric Moody: The 2026 season had everything fantasy managers could ask for, with stars delivering on expectations, breakout players and plenty of help from the waiver wire. With the fantasy season almost over, here are my awards for the players who made the biggest impact.

Fantasy MVP: A'ja Wilson, F/C, Las Vegas Aces

Wilson was the safest player in fantasy and once again delivered elite production across the board. She scored, rebounded, blocked shots and created steals at a level few players could match. Wilson ranks first in total fantasy points and fantasy points per game by a significant margin. If you drafted her at 1.01, she lived up to expectations.

Best scorer award for most fantasy points from points and 3-pointers: Kelsey Mitchell, G, Indiana Fever

Mitchell was one of the league's best sources of scoring and 3-pointers all season. She ranked third in 3-pointers per game while shooting 45.5% from beyond the arc, second in points per game and second in field goal attempts per game. Mitchell ranks fifth in total fantasy points largely because of that scoring production, making her a great return on her average draft position.

Box score award for most fantasy points from rebounds, assists, steals and blocks: Angel Reese, F/C, Atlanta Dream

Reese hasn't had to be a prolific scorer to help fantasy managers. Most of her value comes from everything else. She currently holds the single-season rebounding record, passing A'ja Wilson's mark of 451 from the 2024 season. Reese leads the league in rebounds per game and ranks third in steals per game. When you add in her points, assists and blocks, she ranks fourth in total fantasy points. Reese has generated more value from the non-scoring categories than any other player.

Matchup winner award for best fantasy week: A'ja Wilson, F/C, Las Vegas Aces

Wilson also delivered one of the best fantasy stretches of the season. From July 28 through Aug. 1, she scored 166 fantasy points across three games, including 28 points and 14 rebounds, 33 points with 10 rebounds and six assists, and 36 points with 12 rebounds. A week like that can swing an entire fantasy matchup.

Most underrated award for best player under 50% rostered: Leila Lacan, G, Connecticut Sun

Lacan was one of the better under-the-radar fantasy options this season for a Sun team that was one of the worst in the league. She averaged 23.1 fantasy points in 28.4 minutes per game, and her assists and steals gave her value even when the scoring wasn't there. Despite that production, Lacan remained available in far too many leagues for much of the season.

Others

Biggest rostership rise from opening night to now: Jessica Shepard, F/C, Dallas Wings
Biggest rostership drop from opening night to now: Rickea Jackson, F/C, Chicago Sky

stories.headline: Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle hoping for 'positive' update on Anthony Elanga injury
stories.summary: Matthias Jaissle hopes Anthony Elanga's injury is "not that serious" as Newcastle prepare to face Hull City on Saturday.
stories.body:
Matthias Jaissle hopes Anthony Elanga's injury is "not that serious" as Newcastle prepare to face Hull City on Saturday.

The 24-year-old winger was not included in the matchday squad for Monday's game against Leeds United, which saw Newcastle fall to a 4-1 defeat at Elland Road.

Up next is a test against high-flying Hull at St James' Park and Jaissle is hoping a scan will provide more clarity on Elanga's situation.

"Still not a real update on Anthony. I just spoke with him now. I think in the next 30 minutes he's in the MRI, so we'll get more clarity then and we hope that it's not that serious," Jaissle said.

"It's sad after that great start he had, the team had. We counted on him, definitely, and the way we want to play, it's a key strength in our squad. But we want to stay positive also when he's out.

"Unfortunately then we need to solve it differently, we have the ability in the squad also to adjust things. We believe in our players, we count on the others and that's always a chance for the others."

With the extent of Elanga's issue unknown, there is competition for a spot on the right wing, where Jacob Murphy started on Monday.

However, when posed with the possibility that Amar Dedic could push further up, Jaissle revealed the full-back will also be sidelined for Saturday.

"I have some thoughts on that, but Jacob was doing good," he said.

"Murphy's an experienced player, he's played that role many times. He's also intelligent to know exactly what the gaffer is demanding from him and from him on that position in particular.

"There are other options, not too many at the moment as Amar will be also not available to play on Saturday. So it's getting shorter and shorter the list."

Dedic's absence adds to Newcastle's growing injury concerns as Jacob Ramsey is also set to miss out and Jaissle confirmed he is not expecting any of his currently sidelined players to return for Hull.

Nico González is also not involved on Saturday having been forced off in the 19th minute of the Leeds match after being hit in the head with the ball.

Speaking about Gonzalez, Jaissle said: "It was just unlucky. It was not a big hit but the hit was strong enough and precise enough to knock him out.

"Like I said also in the post-match press conference, we need to be smart.

"We have the responsibility then to follow the protocol from the league, which I really think it's so good that we are so advanced in that approach.

"He's missing Saturday's match but he's feeling much better. He's fine, usually he could train, he can progress but, again, we take that seriously that protocol. Therefore he will be out."

stories.headline: I raced against Max Verstappen ... for 10 seconds: Inside the chaos of Max vs 100
stories.summary: ESPN's Nate Saunders might not have lasted long in Max vs 100, but it was still a memorable event. Here, he reflects on his karting experience with Formula 1's Max Verstappen
stories.body:
Few can say they have raced against Max Verstappen -- even if they can only boast that they stayed in front of him for all of 10 seconds.

That was about as long as my challenge lasted in Max vs 100, a wonderfully simple concept on Disney+: put four-time world champion Verstappen at the back of a 101-kart grid at Silverstone and give him 30 laps to pass everybody in front of him. Once he passed you, your race was over.

Starting 89th, I was eliminated before my kart had even reached the front of the grid we were all racing from.

A humbling experience, no doubt: but should an amateur karter going up against one of the greatest drivers of all time have expected any different?

It wasn't just me who had a blink-and-you-missed-it moment against Verstappen. He dispatched an astonishing 64 drivers in that first lap alone and needed only 13 more to catch and overtake everyone else.

Verstappen enjoyed it so much he teased doing it again next year against 200. Seeing how quickly he got things done on Wednesday, you would not bet against him completing that challenge with a handful of laps to spare, either.

Starting as low as I did, there was probably not much chance of any other outcome for me. I already had the excuses ready to explain my lowly grid slot. A spin during one-shot qualifying had turned what was already a middling-to-below-average lap into one only good enough to occupy the 45th row of the grid. Shoot. A blow, I told myself, of getting down to Turn 1 in one piece and an even bigger blow for my chances of staying ahead of Verstappen for even a few corners. Perhaps a better lap and grid position would have given me a better buffer to prevent the inevitable, I reasoned, while Verstappen struggled to get past the slower karts in the field.

- Max vs 100: Verstappen jokes taking on '200' drivers next time

- Max Verstappen wins Max vs 100 in style after overtaking 100 go-karters

Turns out the excuses weren't necessary -- an improved grid spot wouldn't have made a shred of difference. As the red lights at the beginning of the start procedure went on one by one, Verstappen had rocked his kart backwards and forwards in a bouncing motion, an old trick he said he learned racing as a seven-year-old. It meant his kart was already rolling well enough to breeze past the karts nearest to him as the lights turned green.

I knew no such tricks, so like the majority of the other amateurs, moved off the line sluggishly as I set about looked for a racing line through the blur of cars down towards Turn 1.

Approximately 10 seconds later, as some space opened up around me as I came off the curve and onto the straight, I glanced to my right.

There he was.

And then, he wasn't.

Verstappen breezed on by as though he was driving a different category of vehicle altogether. As that part of the field got to the first corner, karts were spinning left and right, but he threaded through the chaos like a slalom skier, at one stage simply taking to the grass when the conventional route vanished. My own kart got turned around -- perhaps because I was as much watching the disappearing Verstappen as I was the disappearing bit of unoccupied tarmac in front of me. It is easy to forget when watching trackside or TV the remarkable control of a vehicle professionals had -- Verstappen seemed to be racing on rails, even when he was driving off track to pass karts facing the wrong way.

So that was it. 10 seconds after racing Verstappen had started, my race against Verstappen was over. Brutal stuff indeed.

It all happened so fast that some of the 64 who slowly trundled back into the pit lane after elimination were not even convinced they had seen Verstappen go by. By the time I was out of the kart, he was up to 20th.

"I think the first lap went a bit better than expected, so that helps a lot," Verstappen said later.

Organisers had set a limit of 30 laps but that seemed ludicrously generous as he scythed his way through the field. There had been talk beforehand about trying to defend, working together or even making Verstappen fight for each position. When asked about advice for the 100 karters ahead of the event, Verstappen's long-time rival George Russell had joked that participants should try and go four or five-wide and effectively block the road to stop him advancing. There was, of course, not even the slightest bit of coordination between anyone at the back of the field once the lights went out. Even if we had, Verstappen appeared more than happy to take to the grass on a couple of occasions to get to where he needed to be.

"You just act on instinct, whatever happens when the lights go out, you kind of just see where the gaps are and then you also kind of need to trust the few people around you that they don't do anything crazy," Verstappen said later. "But to be honest, they didn't."

Even if no-one was driving like crazy, the chaos at the start was predictable. Race director and circuit designer David Terrien -- who raced against Max's parents Jos Verstappen and Sophie Kumpen when they were junior karters -- later said he doubted there has ever been a kart race featuring 101 karts. That's not surprising, as there did not seem to be quite enough road to accommodate everyone at the beginning. The grid stretched down the main straight and around a curve. The first lap was almost immediately put under caution -- there were spins, mine included, at Turn 1, while two karts crashed at Turn 3 further up the track so badly that a group of 10 karts got stuck behind.

The circuit worked well when the field had been trimmed down, though, with Verstappen's progress slowing as the amateurs on track were wittled down. He spent six laps in fourth, slowly reeling in the runaway trio at the front.

Verstappen ended up beating one journalist who did, at least, manage to do a better job of representing for the F1 paddock: Dutch reporter Jacky Martens, who finished ahead of YouTuber Zac Alsop and Red Bull's own Lewis Osler to be crowned best of the amateurs. Those last laps were entertaining to watch on the stream, as Verstappen got to utilise the microphones he had fitted to his balaclava to talk to the other competitors around him. "I'm coming for you," he said to a contestant at one stage. Later, he told commentators Alex Jacques and Matt Gallagher: "They need to focus because I'm definitely catching them."

Several of those who remained at least got to properly experience what racing Verstappen is all about. Late in the contest, one of the racers joked to Verstappen -- via a microphone which linked the Dutchman to drivers he approached -- that all he could hear in his head was the famous song about him: "Duh Duh Duh Duh, Max Verstappen, Duh Duh Duh Duh."

Another turned to Verstappen as he approached, laughing and putting his hands together as if begging him not to overtake. He's not the only one to have felt like this with the Dutchman approaching him at alarming speed. McLaren CEO Zak Brown joked last year, as Verstappen started reeling in McLaren pair Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri in the championship, that Verstappen was like the T-Rex in Jurassic Park, seen chasing the car in the mirror with the warning 'Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.' My experience of being passed by Verstappen was so quick I didn't even get the chance to experience the fear.

For Verstappen, it seemed like enormous fun -- he later said he had not driven a proper go-kart since 2016. In a year which has seen Verstappen's love of Formula 1 tested on a massive scale, he later joked he would cherish his winners' trophy as it was his first of the year so far.

Verstappen recently signed a contract to stay in Formula 1 with Red Bull into 2030, ending several years of speculation about moves elsewhere. It's perhaps not surprising he can't imagine a future away from the company which first brought him into Formula 1 as a 17-year-old in 2015. "It's just great that with Red Bull they always come up with some crazy fun things and it suits me as well," he said. "I can really be myself and I think also the way it was organised today, I know that it requires a lot of effort to be able to do something like this."

Whether I'll be there on the grid with him for a future event remains to be seen -- if Wednesday's contest had been an audition to race against a Formula 1 legend again, I dismally failed.

But, given how Verstappen did make almost 100 people look like complete amateurs, there doesn't seem to be too much shame in that.

stories.headline: 'Deeper connection': Clark finds true self at Warriors
stories.summary: Warriors lock Erin Clark found form and his identity after his move from the battling Gold Coast to become one of the best players in his position in the NRL.
stories.body:
Erin Clark has emerged as one of the game's best locks and Warriors legend Clinton Toopi says it's due to a re-discovery of who he is as a footballer.

The 29-year-old will start in the No.13 jersey against Newcastle in an elimination final at Eden Park on Sunday a transformed footballer, after being chopped and changed by the underperforming Gold Coast outfit for five seasons.

"When he was at the Titans I think Erin lost his identity in terms of who he is," Toopi told AAP.

"Am I a hooker? Am I a lock? Am I a bench player? Psychologically in those moments you are happy to play anywhere, but when given responsibility to own a starting position it's a huge confidence booster.

"Coach Andrew Webster has got the best out of all the players and Erin has shown that he wants to own that lock position."

In the past two seasons at the Warriors, across 50 games, Auckland-born Clark has averaged 135m compared to the 65m he managed at the Titans.

Incredibly he has notched 2686 post-contact metres in two Warriors seasons, well above the 2113m he made in 94 Titans games.

The New Zealand international started his career in the Warriors system and played NSW Cup in the halves. After playing one NRL game for the club he moved to the Titans where he played well but was never offered a regular starting spot.

After one match off the bench for the Warriors last season, he has played the last 49 in the No.13 jersey without missing a game.

"Erin would admit to that deeper connection coming back home for a second time," Toopi said.

"He has spread his wings and come back and flourished to become one of the game's elite and best in terms of what he offers."

While the Warriors players are part of a tightly run system, Clark naturally has attacking gifts that add to the powerful running and aggressive defence in the middle that has made him such a fearsome proposition.

"In his past he was a little nuggety six but didn't get a chance to play at any stage there with the Titans," Toopi said.

"When you play six for a long time it tells you that you have vision, skill and you are a runner.

"What Erin has been able to do at the Warriors is exploit those talents and show what skillset he can bring to the table. You see him go to the line and get short balls away.

"He has got an offload, he powers through, he has got a flick pass. He has got a grubber. He has been given the OK to do that."

Toopi, who suffered the heartbreak of losing the 2002 decider to the Sydney Roosters, explained what was required in a do-or-die final.

"I got caught up in the atmosphere of the 2002 grand final. You walk out on the field and there are 90,000 going crazy and all I could do was be in awe of the moment," Toopi said.

"Before you know it that 80 minutes is over and you have lost a grand final. It still is very raw 20-odd years later. These Warriors boys will want to walk off the field having no regrets at all."
